summary_responses.response: The Treasury Department's Bureau of the Fiscal Service has issued a final rule amending the Uniform Offering Circular (31 CFR Part 356), which governs auctions of marketable book-entry Treasury bills, notes, and bonds. The amendments take effect October 15, 2026, though the changes to §§ 356.14 and 356.23 will apply starting with the first auction run on Treasury's upgraded auction system. The most substantive change requires submitters of noncompetitive customer bids to provide each customer's name and bid amount before the noncompetitive auction close, ending the use of summary bid amounts, so that auction staff can finish post-auction operations earlier in the day. The rule also makes technical updates: it clarifies definitions such as dated date, issue date, and index ratio without changing inflation-protected securities calculations, removes outdated references (such as paper bids and the former CUSIP issuer's name), and aligns the rules with current terminology like "high yield," "award," and "recognize." Treasury also removed specific references to TreasuryDirect.gov in favor of a general reference to its website, and it said the rule is exempt from notice-and-comment requirements because it relates to contracts, is not a significant or major rule, and involves no collection of information.

summary_responses.response: This paper introduces DiffTry (Differential Retries), a lightweight, stateless mechanism that gives different retry limits to different priority classes of requests in microservice architectures. This turns retries into a rejection-prioritization tool that protects high-value transactions during overloads, whether accidental or caused by attackers flooding the system with cheap low-priority requests. Unlike existing approaches such as local auto-scaling, centralized control (e.g., TopFull), or DAGOR's admission shedding, DiffTry needs no overload detection or coordination between services. It also curbs retry storms and unnecessary over-scaling. The authors build an analytical model, first for a single service using a fluid model and queueing analysis, then for general service networks. It predicts per-class rejection rates, converges with a unique solution for DAG-structured networks, and shows that success rates rise monotonically with retry limits. Simulations and a live Kubernetes deployment, where DiffTry runs as a service-mesh plugin with no application changes, closely match the predictions. In their example, high-priority rejection drops to about 15%, and those requests make up roughly 85% of successful completions.

summary_responses.response: The FAA has issued a final rule, effective November 18, 2026, adopting an airworthiness directive (AD 2026-20-09) for certain Bombardier BD-700-2A12 airplanes after reports of low clearance in the right wing between the fuel line flexible coupling and the harness bracket clip-nut, the fuel line coupling and the hydraulic system, and the hydraulic system and the fuel vent tube. Transport Canada's AD CF-2025-49 warned that these conditions could create an ignition source in the fuel tank during a lightning strike, so the AD requires operators to fix the first two clearance problems, inspect the hydraulic-to-vent-tube clearance, and perform any needed follow-up actions. Of the seven commenters, five supported the proposal unchanged, while one asked why no emergency AD was issued. The FAA answered that the condition would not cause fuel starvation, that the compliance times were adequate based on the manufacturer's risk evaluation, and that no interim measures or further analysis were needed. A second commenter asked the FAA to reopen the comment period or add more material on the incorporated documents and cost assumptions, but the FAA declined, saying the materials meet the "reasonably available" standard and that the cost estimates came from the manufacturer. The AD affects about 60 U.S.-registered aircraft, at an estimated $2,693 per airplane ($161,580 total), plus $5,772 per airplane for any necessary bracket replacements, with some costs possibly covered by warranty.

summary_responses.response: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has issued a direct final rule making technical revisions to its Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations in 5 CFR part 630, subpart L. The revisions incorporate statutory amendments enacted in January 2021 and December 2023, which also affect eligibility for paid parental leave, since that leave is substituted for unpaid FMLA leave. The 2021 amendments make virtually all civilian Federal service, including temporary, intermittent, Postal Service, and non-appropriated fund service, count toward the 12-month eligibility requirement. They also confirm that annual or sick leave earned under non-title 5 authorities can be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave, and they exclude Veterans Health Administration employees covered by a leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 from title 5 FMLA coverage. The 2023 amendment lets honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps count toward the 12-month requirement, but not Coast Guard or Public Health Service commissioned corps service. The rule takes effect December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026, in which case OPM will withdraw the affected provisions and issue a notice of proposed rulemaking.
